lines: Delete a running pod by hand, and watch what happens next.
A new one takes its place almost immediately, without anyone asking for it.
Edit a setting on a live pod, and the same thing happens: it quietly reverts. Something is enforcing a decision you didn't make in that moment.
Three identical pods, managed as one group. Delete one of them by hand.
A minute passes. Nothing you did again, no command you typed a second time.
How many pods are running now, and whose decision was that?
answer: Three again, and it was never your decision to begin with. The group's own controller noticed the gap and closed it.
That deleted pod wasn't special. It was simply the actual count falling short of the declared one, for one tick of a loop that runs constantly.

lines: Separate what's declared from what's actually true right now. Those are two different things, watched by a third thing in between.
That watcher never stops comparing the two, and never waits to be told the gap exists.
Every object in this whole platform works this exact same way underneath.
The smallest unit that actually gets placed somewhere is one of these.
Multiply it by a count, and you get one shape: copies that don't care which one answers a request.

Give each copy its own name and its own storage that follows it around, and you get a completely different shape: ones that are never interchangeable, even though they started from the same blueprint.
Behind one stable name, the thing answering a request can change entirely from one moment to the next.
Whoever's calling that name never has to know, or care, which copy picked up.
Two kinds of configuration object sit right next to each other, and one of them sounds like it protects something.
It doesn't, not by itself. The encoding on that value only disguises it from a glance; it isn't locked away from anyone who already has a way in.
Treat that value as exposed until something else is actually turned on to protect it.

Three roles, and it's worth keeping them apart: one thing already exists and is simply available, one thing is only ever a request for some, and the third is what turns a request into something that actually gets built on demand.
Without that third piece, a human has to pre-build every option by hand before anyone can ask for one.
One mark on a place says: stay out, unless you're explicitly allowed in.
A matching permission lets something past that mark, but notice the word: lets, not forces. Being allowed in is not the same as being sent there.
A completely separate pull, toward or away from a place, is a different decision made on different grounds entirely.
Hold onto that one loop you just learned, because it's the only idea in this whole refresher.
Everything still ahead in this chapter is that identical loop, just looking at a different kind of gap each time.
Notice what none of this told you yet: how much to set aside for any of it, or who gets sacrificed first when a machine runs short.
That's the very next thing.
